messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: negative binomial random number generator
parts:
Hi,

Can somebody advise how to resolve overflow problems with NB random number generator in generated quantities block.  When block is commented out stan code runs fine.  Otherwise it gives an error:
Error : stan::prob::poisson_rng(d): Rate parameter is 1.83399e+009, but must be less than 1.07374e+009
error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

I already set an upper bound on log location as specified in the documentation (2.6.0).

The code is attached.

Thank for advise,
Linas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] negative binomial random number generator
parts:
Nope --- we can't really sample huge values (that's over 1 billion),
because we're using integer arithmetic. The best I could suggest
is either rescaling the (sample with a mean 1/10th or 1/100th
what you want then multiply by 10 or 100 to rescale), or use
a normal approximation.

Or think about reformulating the problem so you're not using
integers so large!

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] negative binomial random number generator
parts:
Bob,

Actually the problem occurs during warmup.  The max data point is 1e+6 so I don't expect that there is a need to sample 1e+9. My non-expert intuition tells me that parameters wary widely during warmup and it happens that eta for neg_binomial_2_log is quite large.  I have constrained it as per documentation with 29log2: vector <upper = 20.1> [N] eta;
However, the error message is for poisson rate parameter.  So I am little bit confused what the constrain should be.

Since there are zeros in the data set I can't use log normal.  
Thank you,
Linas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] negative binomial random number generator
parts:
Try a smaller initial stepsize --- that should stop
the huge swings during warmup.

If you want to constrain, you need to constrain the
argument to the negative binomial RNG. You could
do this with an fmin(1e9, theta), where theta is
the value you're plugging in and 1e9 is a large
legal value --- it will give you the wrong answers,
but if it's just during warmup in exteme cases that
aren't part of the typical set, it won't be a big deal.

- Bob
